name: Double Tower
description: fortified tower in Waterford, Ireland
summary: The Double Tower is one of the 17 towers which were part of the city walls of Waterford, Munster, Ireland. It was built in the latter part of the 15th century and the early part of the 16th century. Six of the original 17 towers survive to this day; the other five being Reginald's Tower, Beach Tower, Semi-Lunar Tower, French Tower, and Watch Tower (Waterford). The Double Tower is located on Castle Street, between the French Tower and the Watch Tower. All three towers are well-preserved, along with some parts of the old city wall between them.

name: Watch Tower
description: fortified tower in Waterford, Ireland
summary: The Watch Tower is a tower on Manor Street in Waterford, Munster, Ireland. It is one of the six surviving towers of the city walls of Waterford. The cylindrical shape of the tower suggests that it was built in the 13th century. The arrow slit openings, or embrasures, with a gun loop at the bottom indicate that the tower was modified in the 15th or 16th century to facilitate artillery operations. The tower does not have any windows on the city side; it was built solely as a defensive structure without a secondary use as a dwelling. At the rear of the tower there are two entrances, one at ground level and another at wall-walk level.

The scar lines of a stone vaulted ceiling over ground floor-level survive in the E and W…

name: Belfast Castle
description: mansion in Cavehill country Park, Belfast, Northern Ireland
summary: Belfast Castle is a mansion located in Cave Hill Country Park in Belfast, Northern Ireland, in a prominent position 400 feet (120 m) above sea level. Its location provides unobstructed views over the City of Belfast and Belfast Lough. There have been several structures called "Belfast Castle" over the centuries, located on different sites. The current "castle" is a Victorian structure that was built between 1867 and 1870 on the slopes of Cave Hill, and it is Grade A listed. The main entrance into the Belfast Castle Demesne is now where Innisfayle Park meets Downview Park West, just off the Antrim Road. The original main entrance into the current demesne was formerly on the Antrim Road…

description: castle in Rathfarnham, South Dublin, Ireland
summary: Rathfarnham Castle is a 16th-century fortified house in Rathfarnham, South Dublin, Ireland. Originally a semi-fortified and battlemented structure, it underwent extensive alterations in the 18th century. It is in the care of the state, has been restored and is open to the public.

name: Swords Castle
description: fortification
summary: Swords Castle is an early medieval castle located in Swords, County Dublin. Originally built for the Archbishops of Dublin in the early 13th century near the Ward River, some of the castle estate had fallen into disrepair by the 14th and 15th centuries. At least partially occupied through the 16th and 17th centuries, the castle was used as a place of rendezvous by Anglo-Irish Catholic families during the 1641 Rebellion. The site was afforded protection as a national monument and placed under the guardianship of the Office of Public Works in the early 20th century. As of the late 20th and early 21st century, the site was subject to a program of "long-term phased restoration", and is…

name: Maynooth Castle
description: castle in County Kildare, Ireland
summary: Maynooth Castle is a ruined castle in Maynooth, County Kildare, Ireland which stands at the entrance to the South Campus of Maynooth University. Constructed in the early 13th century, it became the primary residence of the Kildare Fitzmaurice and Fitzgerald family.

name: Magazine Fort
description: bastion fort and magazine in Dublin, Ireland
summary: The Magazine Fort is a bastion fort and magazine located within the Phoenix Park, in Dublin, Ireland. Built in 1735, it was occupied by British Armed Forces until 1922 when it was turned over to the Irish Defence Forces after the Anglo-Irish Treaty. The Irish Army continued to operate the site as an ammunition store through the mid-20th century. It was fully demilitarised by the 1980s. The fort is now managed by the Office of Public Works. As of 2015, it was in a derelict state and not open to the public, however, some repairs were undertaken and the site partially opened for "limited guided tours" from 2016.

summary: The Spanish Arch and the Caoċ Arch in Galway city, Ireland, are two remaining arches on the Ceann an Bhalla.

name: Scrabo Tower
description: tower in County Down, Northern Ireland
summary: Scrabo Tower is a 135 feet (41 m) high 19th-century lookout tower or folly that stands on Scrabo Hill near Newtownards in County Down, Northern Ireland. It provides wide views and is a landmark that can be seen from afar. It was built as a memorial to Charles Vane, 3rd Marquess of Londonderry and was originally known as the Londonderry Monument. Its architectural style is Scottish Baronial Revival.

name: Burnchurch Castle
description: 15th or 16th century tower house in County Kilkenny, Ireland
summary: Burnchurch Castle is a well-preserved 15th century Norman tower house with a round gate tower, located in the parish of Burnchurch, County Kilkenny, Ireland. Burnchurch Castle and tower, along with the nearby Church of Ireland church and lime trees, became a National Monument in 1993.

A castle of a branch of the Fitzgerald family, styled Barons of Burnchurch in the former county palatinate of Kilkenny. In 1654 the last Baron of Burnchurch, Richard Fitzgerald, was transplanted to Connaught and his possessions granted to Colonel William Warden (Commins 1906, 266). It is claimed that Oliver Cromwell probably stayed in the tower house following the siege of Kilkenny, in March 1650, when his army camped at Burnchurch (ibid.). name: Howth Castle
description: fortification
summary: Howth Castle is a historic dwelling, based on 14th and 15th century Anglo-Norman construction, that lies by the village of Howth, County Dublin, Ireland. It is sited within a substantial estate. The castle was the ancestral home of the St Lawrence family that had held the area since the 12th century Norman invasion, and the head of which held in time the titles of Lord Howth until circa 1425, Baron Howth to 1767, then Earl of Howth until 1909. The castle and estate were held by distaff heirs, the Gaisford-St Lawrence family, from 1909 to 2019, when they were sold to an investment group, Tetrarch.

name: Merlin Park Castle

summary: Merlinpark Castle or Merlin Castle is a tower house and national monument located in County Galway, Ireland, close to the grounds of Merlin Park University Hospital.

name: Ballynacarriga Castle
description: historic site in County Cork, Ireland
summary:
Ballinacarriga Castle is a 16th-century tower house located in the village of Ballinacarriga, about 9 kilometres (5.6 mi) from the town of Dunmanway and 7.5 kilometres from the village of Ballineen. It is a ruin but in good structural condition.
There is also a school nearby.
smr_description: On rocky eminence with good view in all directions, overlooking Ballynacarriga Lough to the SW. This four storey tower house (14.6m E-W; 11.8m N-S) is entered through a rebuilt ground-floor door in the E wall; there is a portcullis slot over the door. A vaulted lobby gives access to a guardroom to the S; the main chamber is to the W; a short flight of steps to the N leads to spiral stair in the NE corner which rises the full height of the tower. The area over the lobby is occupied by six chambers, one above the other; the 1st and 2nd floor are entered from the main chambers; otherwise they are entered from the spiral stairs. Windows have square-set embrasures covered by segmental vaults…

name: Narrow Water Castle
description: 16th-century tower house in Northern Ireland
summary: Narrow Water Castle is a 16th-century tower house and bawn near Warrenpoint in Northern Ireland. It is beside the A2 road and on the County Down bank of the Clanrye (Newry) River, which enters Carlingford Lough 1-mile (1.6 km) to the south. It is a historic monument in state care in the townland of Narrow Water, in Newry and Mourne District Council district, at grid ref: J1256 1939.

name: Reginald's Tower
description: castle in Waterford, Ireland
summary: Reginald's Tower is a historic tower in Waterford, Munster, Ireland. It is located at the eastern end of the city quay. The tower has been in usage for different purposes for many centuries and is an important landmark in Waterford and an important remnant of its medieval urban defence system. It is the oldest civic building in Ireland and it is the only urban monument in Ireland to retain a Norse or Viking name.

Originally developed as a coastal defence fortification in the 16th century to protect upper Cork Harbour and port, the site now houses an observatory, visitor centre and restaurant.

summary: Westport House in Westport, County Mayo, Ireland, is a Georgian country house, historically the family seat of the Marquess of Sligo and the Brownes. The house was designed by the architect Richard Cassels with later additions by Thomas Ivory and James Wyatt.

name: Dunguaire Castle
description: tower house in County Galway, Ireland
summary: Dunguaire Castle is a 16th-century tower house on the southeastern shore of Galway Bay in County Galway, Ireland, near Kinvara. The name derives from the dun (fort) of King Guaire, the legendary king of Connacht.

name: Puck's Castle
description: historic site in County Dublin, Ireland
summary: Puck's Castle is a castle ruin in Rathmichael, County Dublin, Ireland. The castle is thought to have been erected by Peter Talbot in 1537, along with nearby castles on the Pale, to defend from the incursions of the O'Toole clan. The name 'Puck's Castle' is derived from the Celtic folklore spirit the 'Púca', which lends itself to local legend that the castle is haunted.

name: Greencastle

description: castle in County Down, United Kingdom
summary: Greencastle is a castle in County Down, Northern Ireland. While it dates mainly from the 13th century, it had substantial 15th- and 16th-century alterations. It was originally surrounded by outer rectangular walls with four corner towers. It is likely to have been built by Hugh de Lacy, along with Carlingford Castle on the opposite side of Carlingford Lough, to guard the narrow entry channel to the Lough, and the ferry crossing between the two.

name: Bagenal's Castle

description: fortified house in Newry, County Down
summary: Bagenal's Castle is a 16th century fortified house located in Newry, County Down, Northern Ireland. It was rediscovered in 1996, where it was found located in the premises of the former McCann's Bakery. The castle consists of a rectangular plan with three storeys and was made with granite. During its restoration, sandstone was used as the replacement material.

name: Kindlestown Castle
description: castle (hall house) in County Wicklow, Ireland
summary: Kindlestown Castle is a ruined hall house-style castle and a National Monument in Delgany, Ireland.
smr_description: National Monument in state ownership No. 323. Situated in a low-lying area in gently undulating terrain. A rectangular two-storey hall (dims. 21m E-W; 9.8m N-S), of roughly coursed limestone and felsitic rubble, of which only the N wall remains largely intact. It has a barrel-vaulted ground floor, above which the surviving N wall is stepped inward to support the first floor independently of the vault. There are towers at the NW and NE angles which project (L 0.6m) from the N wall; that at the NE has collapsed but the stairwell leading from the ground floor to an intramural passage at first floor level in the N wall is still visible. There is a chamber in the NW tower at this level, with a…

summary: Castle Balfour is a castle situated in Lisnaskea, County Fermanagh, Northern Ireland. It sits at the edge of the parish graveyard just west of Main Street. The castle is a State Care Historic Monument sited in the townland of Castle Balfour Demesne, in the Fermanagh and Omagh district area, at grid ref: H3622 3369.

name: Muckross House
description: public building in Ireland
summary: Muckross House is located on the small Muckross Peninsula between Muckross Lake and Lough Leane, two of the lakes of Killarney, 6 kilometres (3.7 mi) from the town of Killarney in County Kerry, Ireland. In 1932 it was presented by William Bowers Bourn and Arthur Rose Vincent to the Irish nation. It thus became the first National Park in the Irish Free State and formed the basis of the present day Killarney National Park. The house now forms part of a visitor attraction marketed as Muckross House, Gardens and Traditional Farms.

name: Blarney Castle
description: castle in Ireland
summary: Blarney Castle is a medieval stronghold in Blarney, a town in Cork, Ireland. Though earlier fortifications were built on the same spot, the current keep was built by the MacCarthy of Muskerry dynasty, a cadet branch of the Kings of Desmond, and dates from 1446. The Blarney Stone is among the machicolations of the castle.

summary: White's Castle is a 16th-century tower house in Athy, County Kildare, Ireland. Built on the site of an earlier 15th-century castle, White's Castle was built to guard the main river crossing in Athy and was extended over successive centuries.
smr_description: On the E bank of the River Barrow, beside Cromaboo Bridge (KD035-022008-). In 2006 and 2008, Mr. Ben Murtagh was engaged by the owner to conduct a historic building study of the structure and identified at least four construction phases (Murtagh 2011, 145-81). In the primary phase, in the first-half of the 16th-century, a four-storied rectangular (ext. 11.75m N-S; 9.35m E-W) ‘urban tower house’ with battlements and roof was constructed, and now forms the S-half of the present building on the site. Built of quarried roughly dressed grey limestone blocks laid in irregular courses with lime mortar, the walls have a base batter and well-dressed quoins on each corner. Although a modern render…

smr_description: Situated on a low N-S spur in deciduous woodland in a low-lying landscape. This is known as Rathlannon Castle, and it was part of Rathlannon townland until some time after the 1839 ed. of the OS 6-inch map was published. References date from the early 17th century, when it was held by the Esmonds of Johnstown (WX042-017----) (Jeffrey 1979, 31-2), and a castle is depicted on the Down Survey map (1655-8) in the NLI (ms 725; microfilm P7384, N6380) at Rathlannon in Kildavin parish. According to the Civil Survey (1654-5) Marcus Esmond owned 121 acres at Rathlannon in 1641 (Simington 1953, 301), and a John Esmond of Rathlannon was listed for transportation with four dependents in 1653 (Hore…

name: Humewood Castle
description: Castellated house in County Wicklow, Ireland
summary: Humewood Castle is a 32,668 square feet (3,035.0 m2) Gothic-fantasy mansion built in 1870 in 427 acres of parkland at Kiltegan, County Wicklow in Ireland. The mansion was originally built by the English architect William White and extended by James Brooks as a private residence of the Hume family. As of 2024, it is owned by American billionaire John C. Malone.

name: Ballindooly Castle
description: tower house in County Galway, Ireland
smr_description: On E verge of modern road (the older road lay further to W) overlooking Ballindooly Lough to SE. In existence in 1574 when it was in the possession of 'Redmud Reogh' (Nolan 1901, 115). Well-preserved rectangular four-storey tower (L 10.95m, Wth 9m). A pointed-arch doorway of two orders (now robbed) is centrally placed in SE wall: this opens into a lobby with murder-hole above and spiral stairs in E corner. The ground, 1st and 2nd floors are comprised of a main chamber with a subsidiary one to SE. A stone vault exists between 2nd/3rd floors and there is a fireplace in SW wall on 1st floor. An enclosed latrine gallery runs along SE side of the main chamber between lst/2nd floors. There are…

name: Annaghdown Castle
image: Castles of Connacht, Annaghdown, Galway (3) - geograph.org.uk - 4068867.jpg
description: tower house in County Galway
smr_description: On S shore of a small bay on E side of Lough Corrib. Nolan (1901a, 42), quoting from Parker, notes that 'the existence of a castle [GA069-002----] at this spot seems to have sprung from the desire of the Archbishops of Tuam to suppress the bishopric of Annaghdown'. The last bishop was appointed here in 1421 and 'it is to him that the erection of the present castle in probably due' (ibid). In 1574 'Anaghocyne' was in the possession of 'Nicholas Lynch' (Nolan 1901b, 118). An almost square tower (L 11m, Wth 10.3m), in fair condition, it is five storeys high. A pointed arch doorway in SE wall opens into a lobby with a murder-hole above. The guardroom is to S, while a passage to N leads to an…

description: castle in County Tipperary, Ireland
summary: Ormond Castle is a castle on the River Suir on the east side of Carrick-on-Suir, County Tipperary, Ireland. The oldest part of the existing castle is a mid-15th century walled bawn, cornered on the northeast and northwest by towers.

name: Curraghmore House
description: Irish Stately Home
summary: Curraghmore near Portlaw, County Waterford, Ireland, is a historic house and estate and the seat of the Marquess of Waterford. The estate was part of the grant of land made to Sir Roger le Puher by Henry II in 1177 after the Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland. Since then, the De La Poer Beresford family has owned these estates. It is the oldest family home in Ireland.

name: Hillsborough Castle
description: castle in Royal Hillsborough, County Down, Northern Ireland
summary: Hillsborough Castle is an official government residence in Northern Ireland. It is the official residence of the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, and the official residence in Northern Ireland of the British monarch and other members of the British royal family when they visit the region, as well as a guest house for prominent international visitors.

name: Glebe House
smr_description: Part of the monastic complex at Kilmacduagh and situated 100m to the NNE of the cathedral (GA128-034004-). This edifice, now a National Monument, has been variously interpreted as a 'seminary' and/or the residence of the abbot or bishop (Fahey 1904, 230; Harbison 1975, 95). The original building was a rectangular two-storey hall-house (16.2m E-W; 6.7m N-S), aligned roughly E-W, that was accessed via a doorway at 1st-floor level in the S wall. It most likely dates to the 13th century but a number of major alterations are evident, most recently the restoration which involved re-roofing the E half of the building with a gabled roof and crenellated parapet. Only the E jamb of the original…

name: Durrow Castle
description: country house
summary: Castle Durrow is an 18th-century country house in Durrow, County Laois, Ireland. The house was built in the pre-Palladian design and formal gardens that were popular in the 18th century.

name: Fethard Castle
description: 14th-century castle in Fethard-on-Sea, County Wexford, Ireland, which was erected as a summer residence for the bishop of Ferns
smr_description: Traditionally ascribed to the Suttons, whose principal residence was Ballykeerogemore (WX039- 024001-), the castle of Fethard was probably built by the Bishop of Ferns in the 15th century as a summer residence. The manor had been settled on the bishop in 1228-32 by the monks of Christchurch, in Canterbury, in settlement of other claims. The bishop may have made Fethard his summer residence as the castle is designed as two discrete households, which he may have shared with the rector. Thomas Denne, who was bishop from 1363-1400, may have moved the diocesan centre away from Ferns to avoid the Gaelic resurgence, and the castle might date to this episcopate (Colfer 2002, 219). The bishop lived…

name: Cahir Castle
description: castle in Ireland
summary: Cahir Castle, one of the largest castles in Ireland, is sited on an island in the river Suir. It was built from 1142 by Conchobar Ua Briain, King of Thomond. Now situated in Cahir town centre, County Tipperary, the castle is well preserved and has guided tour and audiovisual shows in multiple languages.

smr_description: On the N side of Golden bridge where it crosses a small island in the middle of the River Suir, at the SW end of the village. The present tower house was erected in the late 15th/early 16th century, probably as a Butler stronghold to guard the pass over the River Suir. Barry (1977, 147) suggests that an earlier 12th-14th century stone castle may have occupied this location, however, archaeological excavations in 2003 and 2004 revealed the walls of a substantial 13th/14th building (TS060-097014-) 100m to the E, immediately S of the bridge, which is probably the early castle (Moran 2006, 466-7; 2007, 410). The Civil Survey (1654-6) lists ‘James Earle of Ormond’ as proprietor of ‘Goulden’ in…

name: Clonmacnoise Castle
description: Castle ruin in Clonmacnoise
smr_description: National Monument No. 81. Situated on the low-lying floodplain of the River Shannon which overlooks it to the N. The monastic site (OF005-004----) of Clonmacnoise lies nearby to E. In 1215 Ralph de Derevaus and Walter Reboth who held the custody of the castle of Clonmacnoise were requested to deliver it to Geoffrey de Mariscis (Cal. doc. Ire., 94). The stone castle constructed in the early 13th century comprises a rectangular, three-storey stone keep with adjoining courtyard area, built within a D-shaped earthwork (dims. 32m N-S x 37m E-W) defined by two earthen banks and a wide flat bottomed intervening fosse (Wth 5.9m). The inner bank (Wth 3.7m) is visible at NW only, while the bettere…

name: Classiebawn Castle
description: country house in County Sligo, Ireland
summary: Classiebawn Castle is a country house built for the 3rd Viscount Palmerston (1784–1865) on what was formerly a 4,000-hectare (10,000-acre) estate on the Mullaghmore Peninsula near the village of Cliffoney in County Sligo, Ireland. The current castle was largely built in the late 19th century.

Opened to the public since the 1940s, the house, estate and gardens are a tourist destination in West Cork.

name: Cullahill Castle
description: ruined castle in County Laois, Ireland
summary: Cullahill Castle was the principal stronghold of the MacGillapatricks of Upper Ossory built around 1425 and destroyed around 1650. Cullahill Castle takes its name from an ancient forest that covered Cullahill Mountain and extended down to Cullahill village.
smr_description: Erected by the MacGillapatricks c. 1425; damaged by the Crowellians in the mid seventeenth century and left uninhabitable (Carrigan 1905 vol. 2, 231-3). Built of roughly coursed limestone, this tower house (dims. 15m x 12.6m; wall T 0.95m) is five storeys high with a wall-walk. Most of N portion is missing, as is the doorway. Mural stairwell in NE angle. There is a N-S barrel vault over the ground floor with evidence of a loft which was accessed from an opening in N wall. Mural passage on first and second floors of S wall, and chambers in SE and SW angles, with remains of wicker-centring in SE ones. Large cut-limestone fireplace on second floor of E wall. The third floor was supported on…

smr_description: On a slight limestone eminence, overlooking bridge on the Blackwater River c. 150m to the S. These remains of a fortified house are comprised of a rectangular 3-storey house (int. 25m N-S; 8.3m E-W) with 4-storey towers projecting from the NW and SW corners and from the centre of the E and W walls; the former is polygonal in plan, while the latter have straight sides and pointed front (see plan in Leask 1944, plate 1). The plan by Leask also shows wall foundations within the fortified house but not associated with it, which may be part of the earlier castle of the Fitzgerald earls of Desmond (CO033-009004-) (ibid., 23). The house was built by Sir Thomas Norris, a senior English…

description: castle in Ireland
summary: Athenry Castle is a tower house and National Monument located in Athenry, Ireland.
smr_description: This castle, a conserved National Monument, is situated in the NE end of the Anglo-Norman town of Athenry (GA084-001----). It was built by Meiler de Bermingham between 1235 and 1240 and it occupies a slight rise that controlled a ford over the River Clareen (Bradley and Dunne 1992, 22-3). Rectangular in plan (int. dims. 13.1m NE-SW; 7.25m NW-SE; wall T c. 1.7m) and of random-rubble construction with dressed quoin stones, it is three storeys high with a gabled attic; it has a pronounced base-batter (H 2.1m; base Wth 1.2m). It occupies the W half of the surrounding D-shaped bawn (GA084-001085-), some of the walls of which act as part of the town defences (GA084-001001-). The late Professor…

summary: Portumna Castle is a semi-fortified house in Portumna, County Galway, Ireland which was built in the early 17th century by Richard Burke, 4th Earl of Clanricarde.

name: Claregalway Castle
smr_description: On the site of the medieval borough of Claregalway (GA070-107----): on N bank of the River Clare, 175m ESE of the friary (GA070-035001-) and immediately NE of the modern bridge. A well-preserved rectangular five-storey tower (L c. 12m, Wth c. 9.75m) built in the 15th C by the Clanrickard Burkes (Killanin and Duignan 1967, 162). The original pointed arch doorway is near N end of SE wall. The presence of opposing vertical grooves in both of its jambs indicate that it was protected by a portcullis. This doorway opens into a small lobby with the guardroom to S and the spiral stairs to N. A stone vault exists between 2nd/rd floors. Mural passages occur in NE wall on 1st floor, and in SE wall on…

name: Ashford Castle
description: fortification
summary: Ashford Castle is a mainly Victorian and medieval castle near Cong on the County Mayo–Galway border in Ireland. The castle has been expanded over the centuries and turned into a five star hotel. It is located on the County Galway side of Lough Corrib and was previously owned by the Guinness family.

name: Donegal Castle
description: castle in Donegal County, Ireland
summary: Donegal Castle is a castle situated in the centre of Donegal Town in County Donegal in Ulster, the northern province in Ireland. The castle was the stronghold of the O'Donnell clan, Lords of Tír Conaill and one of the most powerful Gaelic families in Ireland from the 5th to the 16th centuries. For most of the last two centuries, the majority of the buildings lay in ruins but the castle was almost fully restored in the early 1990s. It is now open to the public.

name: Delvin Castle
description: Castle ruin in County Westmeath, Ireland
smr_description: National Monument No. 481. Standing in the town of Delvin on the SE side of the main street with Anglo-Norman motte and bailey castle (WM014-004----) 60m to ESE, church (WM014-003----) 50m to SSW and graveyard (WM014-003001-) 17m to SSW. Sweetman (1999, 95, 99) classified this castle as a hall-house type fortification. McNeill (1997, 150) suggested that the corner towers on Delvin castle could be seen ‘as indicating a link to tower-houses in date’ while he suggested that the second floor may have been added (Ibid., 151). O’Keeffe (2000, 39) considered Delvin Castle to have been constructed in the 15th century / late medieval period. Castle described in the terrier of the 1659 Down Survey…

name: Ross Castle
description: 15th century castle in Ireland
summary: Ross Castle is a 15th-century tower house and keep on the edge of Lough Leane, in Killarney National Park, County Kerry, Ireland. It is the ancestral home of the Chiefs of the Clan O'Donoghue, later associated with the Brownes of Killarney.

smr_description: Usually referred to as 'Taaffe's Castle', it is four storeys high, excluding the wall-walk level, and is constructed of roughly coursed greywacke and limestone rubble and boulders with a very few hammer- or punch-dressed blocks, but with some finely dressed quoin stones. It is rectangular in plan with a westward projecting tower at the SW angle which carries the stairwell. The main doorway, situated in the W end of the S wall, has a two-centred arch constructed of nine large blocks of dressed limestone. The upper parts of the castle are not now generally accessible because it is used as a private warehouse, but it was surveyed by Ms B. Cassidy for a B.A. thesis at Queen's University…

description: castle in County Offaly, Ireland
summary: Charleville Castle is a Gothic-style castle located in County Offaly, Ireland, bordering the town of Tullamore, near the River Clodiagh. It is considered one of the finest of its type in the country.

name: Rockfleet Castle
description: tower house near Newport in County Mayo, Ireland
summary: Rockfleet Castle, or Carrickahowley Castle, is a tower house near Newport in County Mayo, Ireland. It was built in the mid-fifteenth century, and is most famously associated with Grace O'Malley, the 'pirate queen' and chieftain of the Clan O’Malley. The castle has been speculated as her place of death. It is also known as Carraigahowley, which means "rock of the fleet".

name: Audley's Castle
description: Irish Norman ruined tower castle
summary: Audley's Castle is a 15th-century castle located 1 mile (1.6 km) north-east of Strangford, County Down, Northern Ireland, on a rocky height overlooking Strangford Lough. It is a three-storey Tower house named after its 16th century owner, John Audley. Audley's Castle tower house and bawn is a State Care Historic Monument in the townland of Castleward, in Down District Council area, at grid ref: J5781 5058.

name: Castle Ward

name: Doonagore Castle
description: Castle in Ireland
summary: Doonagore Castle is a round 16th-century tower house with a small walled enclosure located about 1 km south of the coastal village of Doolin in County Clare, Ireland. Its name may be derived from Dún na Gabhair, meaning "the fort of the rounded hills" or the "fort of the goats". Doonagore Castle is at present a private holiday home, inaccessible to the public.
smr_description: On a natural rise in hilly pastureland, situated midway along the SE wall of a bawn (CL008-087002-). Overlooked by higher ground to S and SE, but otherwise commanding a panoramic view. Named ‘Doonnagore Castle (in Ruins)’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Probably built by the O’Connors in the 14th/15th century, by 1570 the castle was under the ownership of Sir Donnel O’Brien. In 1582 Brian MacCahill O’Connor was recorded as the owner, suggesting that perhaps the O’Connors were still living there under the O’Briens (Ua Cróinín and Breen 1997). Toward the end of that century the castle became a possession and residence of the MacClancy family, brehons of the O’Briens of…

name: Avondale House
description: house

It is set in the Avondale Forest Park, spanning over 2 km2 of land, approximately 1.5 km from the nearby town of Rathdrum. The river Avonmore flows through the park on its way towards the Irish Sea. The house is now a museum.

name: Barntown Castle (ruins)

description: tower house in County Wexford, Ireland
summary: Barntown Castle is a tower house near Wexford town in Ireland. It is about 5 kilometres (3 mi) west of the centre of Wexford town, on the main Wexford to New Ross road. The castle, set in the middle of a grazing field, is now in ruins and used as a cattle shelter. A Georgian mansion has replaced the castle as the residence of the local landowners, currently the Joyce family.
smr_description: References date from 1562 when an inquisition reported that it had been held by Walter Roche who had died the previous year and whose heir was William Wadding. A John Wadding held it in 1635 (Jeffrey 1979, 98-9) but in 1641 the ruined castle and 210 acres at Barntown was held by Robert Roche and John Wadding (Simington 1953, 106). The latter was listed (1655-9) to receive 216 acres in Connaught (Hore 1900-11, vol. 6, 505). The tower house is located towards the bottom of the N-facing slope at the N end of the NE-SW ridge of Forth Mountain. This is a rectangular tower (ext. dims 7.9m N S; 6.6m E W) of five storeys with a destroyed N-S vault over the first floor. It survives to the base of…

The name had changed to Adamstown by the late 16th century and the tower house was built by Nicholas Devereux and his wife Katherine, the daughter of Sir Richard Power of Curraghmore, Co. summary: Tellarought Castle is a fortified tower house located approximately 11 km (7 mi) south-east of New Ross, County Wexford, Ireland.
smr_description: The Sutton family held two cartrons in Carnagh in 1307 (Orpen 1934, 60) and they presumably held them at end of the 16th century, but the property had passed to a Matthew Forde by 1641 (Jeffrey 1979, 170-71). According to the Civil Survey (1654-6) Mathew Forde owned a castle in disrepair and 360 acres in the townlands of Aclamon and Tellarought in Carnagh parish in 1641 (Simington 1953, 186). The four-storey tower house is located on the floor of a slight N-S valley with a small stream c. 40m to the W and it is on the NW side of a NE-SW road. The tower (ext. dims. 7.4m N-S; 7.3m E-W) is vaulted over the first floor, and has good quoins and a base-batter. There are murder-holes inside and…

name: Castlegar Castle
image: Castles of Connacht, Castlegar, Galway (1) - geograph.org.uk - 4068882.jpg
smr_description: On a raised platform on the crest of a S-facing slope, in the house cluster of Castlegar, overlooking the headwaters of the Terry land River. In existence in 1574 when it was in the possession of 'Rolland Skeret' (Nolan 1901, 115). Rectangular four-storey tower (L c. 9.3m, Wth 7.5m) in fair condition: most of SE and SW walls are gone. However, sufficient remains to indicate the position of the doorway in SE wall. The stairwell was in the SE corner. The ground, 1st and 2nd floors each comprised a main chamber with a subsidiary one to SE. A stone vault existed between 3rd/4th storeys and there is an exit to a latrine chute at the base of NW wall. A possibly concealed chamber existed beneath…

name: Ballyhack Castle
description: tower house in County Wexford, Ireland
smr_description: The church of Balishauc was confirmed to the Knights Hospitallers of St. John of Jerusalem in 1212, and this name has been mistakenly interpreted as Ballyhack (Hore 1900-11, vol. 3, 241-50; Moore 1996, 168, No. 1503), but Balishauc is now identified as Ballyhoge parish in Shelmaliere and Bantry baronies (Colfer 2002, 202-05). Ballyhack was within the Cistercian estate of Dunbrody Abbey (WX039-030001-) and would have been built in the 15th century to protect its fishing community and the ferry with Passage East. At the Suppression in 1541 Dunbrody abbey held nine tenements at Ballyhack (Hore 1900-11, vol. 3, 126). The tower house is a National Monument (Harbison 1970, 245), and is open to…

name: Reynolds Castle
smr_description: Situated in woodland c. 25m from the E shore of Lough Rinn, which is described as ‘Clam Lough’ on the Down Survey (1656-8) barony map where the castle is depicted as what might be two towers. The house of Mael Sechlainn MacRaighnaill was attacked by Tadhg MacRaighnall in 1473 when fourteen men were killed (AC), and this is thought to be at Lough Rinn (Mc Carthy 1989-90, 126). It is described as a castle ruin on an estate map (Wogan 1750, 22), and the terrier or commentary suggests that it might be easily repaired. This might have been done as the remains have been conserved. The castle is a rectangular structure (ext. dims 10m N-S; 7m E-W) with battered walls and rounded corners, surviving…

name: Kilcloggan Castle
image: Castles of Leinster, Kilcloggan, Wexford (2) - geograph.org.uk - 3036302.jpg
smr_description: Located at the bottom of a slight S-facing slope. A preceptory of Knights Templar, known as Kilcloggan, is traditionally said to have been founded by O'More of Laois in the late 12th century (Redmond 1900, 220-5; Gywnn and Hadcock 1970, 330), but is more likely to have been based on a grant of the church of St. Alloch by Henry II in 1172 (Colfer 2002, 196). The grant comprised the parishes of Hook and Templetown. Allock or Eallóg (Doologe) was a son of Díona, daughter of a Saxon king, and Brachan, a Welsh king (Ó Rian 2011, 280-1). The name Kicloggan is a corruption of Cill Eallóg – Alloch’s church. When the Templars were suppressed after 1312, much of their property, including Kilcloggan…

name: Slade Castle
description: tower house in County Wexford, Ireland
summary: Slade Castle is a tower house and National Monument in County Wexford, Ireland. It is located in the village of Slade on the Hook Peninsula and primarily dates to the late 15th or early 16th century.
smr_description: Situated on the S side of the harbour at Slade, on the E side of the low-lying and narrow part (L c. 4.5km NE-SW; Wth c. 600m-1.5km NW-SE) of the Hook peninsula. References to the Laffans of Slade date from 1541 but this Irish family was in the county from at least 1376 when Thomas Laffan of Ross, an Irishman, was granted the benefit of English law, in confirmation of an earlier mandate to William Naffan in 1279 (Hore 1900-11, vol. 4, 419-20). At the Suppression of the Knights Hospitallers’ manor of Kilcloggan (WX049-004----) in 1541 Nicholas Laffan held 120 acres in Hooke parish from them (White 1943, 101). Nicholas died in 1567, and in 1581 Joan Laffan, probably Nicholas’ widow, is…

name: Dunamon Castle
description: Fortified house in County Roscommon, Ireland
summary: Donamon Castle, or more correctly, Dunamon Castle, is one of the oldest inhabited buildings in Ireland and stands on raised ground overlooking the River Suck in County Roscommon.
smr_description: Dún Iomain or Dún Imghain, where Turlough O'Conor built a fort, was burnt by Muirchartach Ua Lochlainn in 1154 (AFM vol. 2, 1113). The O'Finaghty of Clanconway, a territory W of the Suck, were dispossessed in the 13th century when Adam Staunton erected a castle, probably an earthwork castle, here in 1232 which was destroyed by Felim O'Conor in 1233. In 1283 a castle was built by John de Stanford (Graham 1988, 31; Lynn 1986, 101) which passed to the Berminghams before passing to the Burkes c. 1310, when it became a centre of the Mac David Burkes. It was captured by Aodh Mac an Abbot O'Conor in 1400. Up to this it may have been an earthen ringwork castle but the present structure may have…

References to the Whitty family of Ballyteige as vassals of the Marshalls and their heirs date from the early 13th century when they also held land in Waterford from the King. Robert de Wythay held Ballythayk by half a knight’s fee from the Valence estate in 1247, and Richard Wytteye held Ballytayk in 1324 by the same fee. Almost all the Whitty owners can be traced, and around 1425 Ballycage was held by Robert Whitty, who was Bishop of Ferns (1415-57) (Brooks 1950, 113-5). Art Mac Murrough Kavanagh burned a castle at Ballyteige in 1408 (Jeffrey 1979, 61 3), and the tower house may have been built as a replacement after that date. Richard Whitty died in 1539 and his son, Robert, a minor…

name: Belle Isle Castle
description: historic Irish landmark situated on Belle Island
summary: Belle Isle Castle is an 18th-century house on Belle Isle, an island previously known, in Gaelic times, as Ballymacmanus Island or Senadh-Mic-Maghnusa or, simply, Senad. The Belle Isle Estate stretches over 470-acres near Lisbellaw in County Fermanagh, Northern Ireland.

description: tower house in County Wexford, Ireland
smr_description: References to the Cheevers of Bailyhealy date from the 13th century. They may have been descended from Sir Harmmond Cheevers of Cheevers Manor, Norfolk, and ultimately from the lordship of Chievres in the Duchy of Lorraine (Jeffrey 1979, 56). William Chevre witnessed William Marshal’s charter to Tintern abbey in 1207-1213 (Hore 1900-11, vol. 2, 23). Nicholas Chever held Ballydufathely by half a knight’s fee from the Bigod estate in 1247, and Patrick Chevre held Balydoftanly by the same fee in 1307 (Brooks 1950, 33-4). In 1314 Nicholas Chevres inherited lands at Balycoloun, which is identified as Cullenstown in Bannow parish, and this is combined with Balyduhaly as possessions of William…

smr_description: Situated on a broad rise in a fairly level landscape. It is described as a castle in ruins on the 1839 ed. of the OS 6-inch map. Mulrankin was held by the Brown family from the 13th century at least (Brooks 1950, 34-5), but their main centre in the later middle ages was Mulrankin castle (WX047-031----). Rathronan, which is within the parish but c. 1.5km NW of Mulrankin, was probably established for a younger branch of the family. Nicholas Browne of Rathronan was listed as a gentleman in 1608, and in 1633 Nicholas Brown of Rathronan or Ballycrosse possessed 60 acres at Ballycrosse (Jeffrey 1979, 87). According to the Civil Survey (1654-6) Thomas Browne owned 60 acres and the castle at…

name: Clifden Castle
description: Castle in County Galway, Ireland
summary: Clifden Castle is a ruined manor house west of the town of Clifden in the Connemara region of County Galway, Ireland. It was built c. 1818 for John D'Arcy, the local landowner, in the Gothic Revival style. It fell into disrepair after becoming uninhabited in 1894. In 1935, ownership passed to a group of tenants, who were to own it jointly, and it quickly became a ruin.

smr_description: Situated on a slight rise overlooking the headwaters of a small N-S stream that is c. 400m to the SE. References to the Wadding family in Co. Wexford date from the mid 14th century when Robert Waddynge was Sergeant of Wexford in 1356-7, Thomas was Sheriff in 1383, and David was sheriff in 1398 and again in 1413. Richard Wadding possessed the castle and land of Ballycogly at his death in 1585 (Jeffrey 1979, 2-3). Anastasia Rossiter of Rathmacknee (WX042-029001-) marrired James Wadding and their son, Luke, was Catholic bishop of Ferns 1678-1687, in succession to his cousin, Nicholas French of Ballytory (WX048042----) (Redmond 1898). According to the Books of Survey and Distribution Richard…

name: Dún na Station castle
description: 17th century castle in Baltimore, Ireland
summary: Dunasead Castle, sometimes known as Baltimore Castle, is a 17th-century fortified house situated in the town of Baltimore in County Cork, Ireland. The tower house is built on the site of an earlier Norman-era structure, which itself replaced an earlier Bronze Age ringfort. Traditionally associated with the chiefs of clan O'Driscoll, the castle was purchased and restored by members of the McCarthy family in the late 1990s, and partially opened to the public from 2005.

smr_description: Situated on a slight N-facing slope on the S side of the W-E Nanny River, with the stream c. 550-650m to the N. A three storey, four bay house was built onto the SW wall of the tower house (ME027-013----) in the seventeenth century, and a NW-SE wing was added to its SW end, probably in the 18th century. The original ornate doorway to the seventeenth century wing is at the S end of the SE wall, and on the ground floor a passage leads past four rooms to a doorway in the S tower of the tower house. At the first and second floors the passages are on the NW side of the house but do not communicate with the tower house. The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory…

name: Clonony Castle
smr_description: Situated on top of natural rock outcrop in undulating countryside. Three storey tower (10.75m E-W; 8.2m N-S; wall T 2.1m) built with roughly coursed limestone rubble entered through a rebuilt door in the W wall which is protected by a machicolation now destroyed at wall-walk level with a later inserted window directly below. Inside door there is a murder-hole above with an intramural chamber which is accessed from the first floor. Spiral stairs in the SW angle from which all main chambers are accessed. The main chamber at ground floor level is accessed from the lobby area via a two centred pointed door with finely punch dressed jambs. The vaulted first floor gives access to a garderobe…

name: Leamaneh Castle
description: castle ruin in County Clare, Ireland
summary: Leamaneh Castle is a ruined castle located in the townland of Leamaneh North, parish of Kilnaboy, between the villages of Corofin and Kilfenora at the border of the region known as the Burren in County Clare, Ireland. It consists of a 15th-century tower house and a 17th-century mansion.

name: Killyleagh Castle
description: castle in the village of Killyleagh, Northern Ireland
summary: Killyleagh Castle is a castle in the village of Killyleagh, County Down, Northern Ireland. It is believed to be one of the oldest inhabited castles in the country, with parts dating back to 1180. It follows the architectural style of a Loire Valley château, being redesigned by the architect Sir Charles Lanyon in the mid-19th century. It has been owned by the Hamilton family since the early 17th century.

name: Mount Stewart
description: Historic house museum and garden in Co. Down, Northern Ireland
summary: Mount Stewart is a 19th-century house and garden in County Down, Northern Ireland, owned by the National Trust. Situated on the east shore of Strangford Lough, a few miles outside the town of Newtownards and near Greyabbey, it was the Irish seat of the Stewart family, Marquesses of Londonderry. Prominently associated in particular with the 2nd Marquess of Londonderry, Britain's Foreign Secretary at the Congress of Vienna, and with the 7th Marquess of Londonderry, the former Air Minister who at Mount Stewart attempted private diplomacy with Hitler's Germany, the house and its contents reflect the history of the family's leading role in social and political life in Britain and Ireland.

description: ruined fortified house in County Cork, Ireland
summary: Coppingers Court is a ruined four-storey fortified house dating from 1616, situated on private property approximately 1 kilometre (0.6 mi) from the sea. It was built by Sir Walter Coppinger and located in Ballyvireen valley, west of Rosscarbery in County Cork, Ireland. The house has a rectangular centre flanked by two wings on the east and west, resulting in a total of 9 gables.

name: Dunlough Castle
description: Norman fortification in County Cork, Ireland
summary: Dunlough Castle, standing atop the cliffs at the northern tip of the Mizen Peninsula, looks at the Atlantic Ocean from the extreme southwest point of Ireland. Founded in 1207 by Donagh O’Mahony, Dunlough is one of the oldest castles in Ireland and an example of Norman architecture and dry stone masonry.

name: Ayesha Castle
description: castle in Ireland
summary: Manderley Castle, formerly "Victoria Castle" and "Ayesha Castle," is a large castellated Irish mansion built in Victorian style, in Killiney, County Dublin, Ireland. It has been owned by musician Enya since 1997.

name: Darver Castle
description: castle in Ireland
summary: Darver Castle is a fortified tower and manor house located in Readypenny, Dundalk, County Louth, Ireland, dating back to the 12th century. The name "Darver" is derived from the Gaelic word "Dairbhe" meaning "Oakwood."

name: Gleninagh Castle
description: castle in County Clare
summary: Gleninagh or Glaninagh is a civil parish in County Clare, Ireland. It lies in the extreme northwest of the Burren, on the south of the mouth of Galway Bay. It is known for the well-preserved L-plan Gleninagh Castle, a 16th-century tower house. The parish also contains the lighthouse on Black Head.

name: Malahide Castle
description: castle near the village of Malahide, Ireland
summary: Malahide Castle, parts of which date to the 12th century, lies close to the village of Malahide, 14 km north of central Dublin in Ireland. It has over 267 acres (1.08 km2) of remaining parkland estate, forming the Malahide Demesne Regional Park.

name: Dunsany Castle
description: castle begun 12th century, in continuous ownership, County Meath, Ireland
summary: Dunsany Castle, Dunsany, County Meath, Ireland, is a modernised Anglo-Norman castle, started c. 1180 / 1181 by Hugh de Lacy, who also commissioned the original Killeen Castle, nearby, and the famous Trim Castle. It is one of Ireland's oldest homes in continuous occupation, possibly the longest occupied by a single family, having been held by the Cusack family and their descendants by marriage, the Plunketts, from foundation to the present day. The castle is surrounded by its demesne, the inner part of the formerly extensive Dunsany Estate. The demesne holds a historic church, a walled garden, a stone farm complex, and an ice house, among other features, and is home to a wide range of fauna.

name: Slane Castle
description: Castle in Ireland
summary: Slane Castle is located in the village of Slane, within the Boyne Valley of County Meath, Ireland. The castle has been the family seat of the Conyngham family since it was built in the late 18th century, on land first purchased in 1703 by Brig.-Gen. Henry Conyngham.

smr_description: In bogland on a low spur of outcropping limestone that separates Lough Doo to the W and Lough Aslaun to the E. This well-preserved and partially restored tower house (11.9m N-S; 8.7m E-W), which is a National Monument, was in existence in 1574 when it was in the possession of 'John Oshagnes' (Nolan 1901, 114); it remained in O'Shaughnessy ownership until 1697 when it was confiscated (Harbison 1975, 91). The tower is six-storeys high with a gabled roof and a slight base-batter. It is protected by two bawns (GA128-052001- and GA128-052002-) and is centrally located in the inner one. It is accessed by a pointed arched doorway in the N wall, which leads to a small lobby with a murder-hole…

description: house in Caledon, County Tyrone, Northern Ireland
summary: Caledon House, also called Caledon Castle, is a country house near the town of Caledon, County Tyrone, Northern Ireland. Caledon House sits on the private 3,000-acre woodland estate of the Earls of Caledon. For more than 200 years, the estate has been maintained as the private home of the aristocratic Alexander family.

summary: Barmeath Castle is a country house near Dunleer in the centre of County Louth. Of note are the castle's 10 acres of gardens designed by the 18th-century landscape architect Thomas Wright.

name: Glin Castle
description: country house in County Limerick, Ireland
summary: Glin Castle is a Georgian country house and protected structure located along the River Shannon in Glin, County Limerick, Ireland. It was built in the late 18th century to replace an earlier tower house of the same name. The estate has belonged to the FitzMaurice/FitzGerald family for over 700 years and was the seat of the Knights of Glin.

name: Carrick Castle
description: castle in County Kildare, Ireland
smr_description: Prominently sited on the upper, S-facing slope of Carrick Hill. A medieval church (KD002-010002-) and graveyard (KD002-010003-) stand 40m to SE. The monument comprises the poorly preserved remains of a possible late-13th/14th-century hall-house with a later tower attached at SE. The remains consist of the short, conjoined portions of the NE wall (int. L 6.8m; T 1.3m) and SE wall (int. L 3.3m; T 1.7m) of a three-story hall-house (the upper story a later addition) built of unbattered, randomly coursed, rounded granite blocks, on a plinth visible at the NW end of the NE wall (traceable L 1.5m; projects 0.3m NE), and orientated on a NW-SE axis; with a later, four- story rectangular tower…

name: Listowel Castle
description: Castle in County Kerry, Ireland
summary: Listowel Castle, located near the town of Listowel, County Kerry in Ireland, was built in the 15th century. The castle is a noted example of Anglo-Norman architecture in County Kerry, and has been the subject of several restoration projects. It is now protected as a national monument, and is open to the public for tours on a daily basis.
smr_description: National Monument No. 260. Situated on the E bank of the River Feale, Listowel Castle, the residence of the Fitzmaurice (Mac Maurice) Clan, Lords of Kerry, originally extended from its present position to the river's edge, but this section was demolished. The present fabric of the castle dates probably to the 15th century. The castle stands on the SW side of The Square in the town of Listowel, 25m to the E of the River Feale, with mill 35m to S, medieval church (KE010-061----) and graveyard (KE010-061001-) 600m to the NE. description: castle in County Tipperary, Ireland
summary: Loughmoe Castle is a ruined castle in County Tipperary, Ireland. It is by Loughmore village, 4 km south of Templemore. The castle was the ancestral home of the Purcell family, the Barons of Loughmoe.
smr_description: Situated on flat pasture with good views in all directions. 'Theobald Purcell of Loghmoe Esqr. Irish Papist' is listed as proprietor in 1640 and the house is described as 'a large demolished stone house' (Simington 1931, vol.1, 69). A seventeenth-century Z-plan house which was added to the N façade of an adjoining tower house (TN035-030005). The house consists of a central rectangular block (ext. dims. 10.2m E-W; 26.7m N-S; wall T 1.1m) which is four storeys high with attic over a semi-basement and has a five-storey angle tower at the NW and SE angles. The main block is a single pile construction possibly divided into three rooms at each level by wooden partitioning. There are two…

name: Castle Donovan
description: Ruined castle in Cork, Ireland
summary: Castle Donovan or Castledonovan or O'Donovan's Castle refer to the remains of an Irish tower house or túrtheach, in a valley near Drimoleague, of medium size which was the so-called "seat" of the Clann Cathail sept of the O'Donovans for a period during the 16th century. The original name of the castle, and when the O'Donovans were actually living in it, was Sowagh before the 17th century. The name of Castle Donovan, after the Manor of the Castle of O'Donovan, is associated with a regrant from James II of England in 1615. Approximately 60 feet in height, it sits on a large rock or outcropping, which forms the ground floor, close to the bank of the River Ilen. It is commonly believed to have…

name: O'Dea Castle
description: castle in Ireland
summary: O'Dea Castle, also known as Dysert O'Dea Castle, is an Irish fortified tower house, loosely described as a castle at Dysert O'Dea, the former O'Dea clan stronghold, 5 kilometres (3 mi) from Corofin, County Clare. It was built between 1470 and 1490 by Diarmaid O'Dea, Lord of Cineal Fearmaic, and stands some 50 feet (15 m) high on a limestone outcrop base measuring 20 by 40 feet. The tower is adjacent to Dysert O'Dea Monastery, close to the R476 road.

name: Kinbane Castle
description: Castle in County Antrim, Northern Ireland
summary: Kinbane Castle is located in County Antrim, Northern Ireland, on a headland between Ballycastle and Ballintoy. The name comes from the Irish for "white head", referring to the limestone of the promontory. Nowadays, the castle is largely destroyed. Kinbane Castle is a State Care Historic Monument sited in the townland of Cregganboy, in Moyle District Council area, at grid ref: D0876 4383. The area surrounding Kinbane Castle is a Scheduled Historic Monument, grid ref: D0879 4381. The site also has views of Rathlin Island and Dunagregor Iron Age fort.

name: Ballycarbery Castle
description: castle in County Kerry, Ireland
summary: Ballycarbery Castle is a castle 3 kilometres (2 mi) from Cahersiveen, County Kerry, Ireland. The castle is high on a grass hill facing the sea and is a short distance from Cahergall Fort and Leacanabuile Fort.

name: Dunluce Castle
description: on north Irish coast
summary: Dunluce Castle is a now-ruined medieval castle in Northern Ireland, the seat of Clan MacQuillan. It is located on the edge of a basalt outcropping in County Antrim, and is accessible via a bridge connecting it to the mainland. The castle is surrounded by extremely steep drops on either side, which may have been an important factor to the early Christians and Vikings who were drawn to this place where an early Irish fort once stood.

name: Castle Oliver
description: Castle in County Limerick, Ireland
summary: Castle Oliver is a Victorian castle-style country house in the southern part of County Limerick, Ireland. Built for entertaining rather than for defense, it has a ballroom, drawing room, library, morning room, dining room and hall which feature hand-painted ceilings, decorated ornamental corbels, superbly executed stained glass windows and stencil work. The castle stands on massive terraces and has a commanding view over much of its former 20,000-acre (81 km2) estate. The castle has Ireland's largest wine cellar, said to hold approximately 55,000 bottles.

name: Clara Castle
description: tower house and National Monument located in County Kilkenny, Ireland
summary: Clara Castle is a tower house (caiseal) located in County Kilkenny, Ireland.
smr_description: On level ground in a small river valley with a stream running roughly N-S c. 100m to the E. The view is restricted E by Grange Hill and to the N by Oliver’s Hill. There is a good view elsewhere with Freestone Hill visible to the SE. The castle was built by the Shortall family who were associated with Clara Upper since the 13th century (Carrigan 1905, vol. 3, 357). In 1596 Nicholas Shortall resided at Clara Upper and following his death in 1600 it was inherited by his brother Patrick and thence, upon his death in 1628, to his son Oliver Shortall (ibid. 357-8). The Shortall family appear to have been in their possession until sometime before 1642 (Leask 1937, 284). Following the Cromwellian…

name: Shane's Castle
description: country house in Antrim, County Antrim, Northern Ireland
summary: Shane's Castle is a ruined castle near Antrim in Northern Ireland, which was mostly destroyed in 1816 by fire. The castle is situated on the north-east shores of Lough Neagh, 2.7 miles from Randalstown. Built in 1345 by a member of the Clandeboy O'Neill dynasty, it was originally known as Edenduffcarrick, meaning "brow of black rock". It owes its present name to Shane McBrian McPhelim O'Neill, who ruled Lower Clandeboy between 1595 and 1617.

summary: McDermott's Castle is a castle and protected national monument located in County Roscommon, Ireland. The site of a fortification since at least the 13th century, the structure's tower house may date from the 16th century, with much of the current building dating to the 19th century.
smr_description: Known as Mac Dermot's Rock or Castle Island (Weld 1832, 238-9), it was a centre of the Mac Dermot clan and seems to have been the symbol of sovereignty amongst them as possession of the Rock was hotly contested throughout the Middle Ages. The character of the remains have been much debated (Lynn 1985-6, 104; Graham 1988, 33; Doran 2005, 382-3). The fortification may have been constructed of wood originally and it cannot be stated definitively when or by whom the present remains were constructed, although the tower house (RO006-046001-) may be the 'great regal house' begun by Brian Mac Dermot (KM 1585-92) in 1578 (ALC, vol. 2, 423). name: Ardfinnan Castle
image: Castles of Munster - Ardfinnan, Tipperary (2) - geograph.org.uk - 1393369.jpg
description: Castle in Ireland
summary: Ardfinnan Castle, is a castle built in 1185 with its sister Lismore Castle, by the river crossing at Ardfinnan in County Tipperary, Ireland. It is situated on the River Suir, four miles south of Cahir and seven miles west of Clonmel. One of the earliest Norman castles in Ireland, Ardfinnan and Lismore represent the oldest castles built by the Norman Crown in Ireland. The castle and grounds are a private residence and not open for public viewing.

smr_description: On a SW-facing slope, c. 200m N of the Kings River, commanding a good view E-S-W at ground level. description: Tower house in County Kilkenny, Ireland
summary: Kilbline Castle is a fortified 16th century tower house in County Kilkenny in Ireland. It is set on the Kilbline Estate in the parish of Tullaherin, within the historical barony Gowran, approximately 1 mile southeast of Bennettsbridge. It is recorded as a protected (listed) structure by Kilkenny County Council.
smr_description: On a slight elevation in good undulating pasture, with farm house attached to the N and farmyard to the E. The lands of Kilbline were among the possessions of Thomas Comerford of Ballymack and were confiscated when he was attainted for rebellion in 1566 (Carrigan 1905, vol. 3, 485). These possessions were leased to James Prescott in 1577 (Fiant Eliz. 3012), to Francis Lovell in 1583 (Fiant Eliz. 4267) and finally were granted to Henry Comerford in 1586 (Fiant Eliz. 4909). Kilbline passed to the Shortall family in or by 1586, in which year the castle is first mentioned (Carrigan 1905, vol. 3, 485). In the Down Survey (1655-6) it is described as ‘a castle in good repaire and a pigeon house’…

description: tower house in Ballybur Upper, Co. Kilkenny
smr_description: On a slight rise of ground with good views in all directions. Ballybur tower house is located in the townland previously known as Ballymackan. The construction of the tower house is attributed to Thomas Comerford, who died in 1588, and was the head of the Comerford family of Ballybur (Hogan 1880-83, 40-41). His son, Richard Comerford (1564-1637), was probably responsible for remodelling the castle, with the insertion of new windows and fireplaces in the upper storeys. name: Mahee Castle
description: castle in the UK
summary: Mahee Castle, also known as Nendrum Castle, is a small ruined tower house near Nendrum Monastery on Mahee Island in Strangford Lough, County Down, Northern Ireland. It was built in 1570 by Captain Thomas Browne. It was abandoned by the early 17th century, and fell into disrepair. In 1923, H.C. Lawlor and the Belfast Natural History and Philosophical Society partly renovated the tower house to avoid further erosion and built a buttress wall to support the northwest corner of the tower.

name: Drenagh
description: country house in Limavady, County Londonderry, Northern Ireland
summary: Drenagh is a 19th-century house and gardens in Limavady, County Londonderry, Northern Ireland. Drenagh has been the home of the McCausland family since 1729, and the present house was built in 1835. It was the first major work by Charles Lanyon, known for his work in Belfast. The gardens include features from the 18th century, as well as an extensive 19th-century Italian garden and elements added in the 1960s. The house is a Grade A listed building.

name: Geneva Barracks
description: barracks in County Waterford, Ireland
summary: Geneva Barracks in County Waterford, Ireland, was a barracks created in 1783 by converting a settlement which had been created for an 18th-century colony of disaffected citizens of Geneva following the Geneva Revolution of 1782. Built near Passage East, the colony was commissioned by the Irish Parliament and approved by the Crown. After the Genevans abandoned their plans to settle in Waterford, the colony became a military barracks instead. During the Irish Rebellion of 1798, the barracks was transformed into a holding centre for captured United Irishmen rebels, many of whom were executed, transported or conscripted. Today, the only remains of New Geneva are its ruined walls in a grassy…

name: Altinaghree Castle

summary: Altinaghree Castle or Liscloon House, known locally as Ogilby's Castle, is a large, derelict building situated outside Donemana, County Tyrone, Northern Ireland. It is believed to have been built around 1860 by William Ogilby.

name: Derg Castle
description: Irish Castle
summary: Derg Castle, also called Castlederg Castle, is a post-medieval ruined fortification, situated on the north bank of the River Derg, within the town of Castlederg, in County Tyrone, Northern Ireland. It has given the town its name: 'Castlederg' derives from the Irish Caisleán na Deirge, meaning 'Castle on the Derg'.

name: Moyry Castle
description: castle in Northern Ireland
summary: Moyry Castle is a small 17th century castle in County Armagh, Northern Ireland. It was built during the latter stages of the Nine Years' War in June 1601 by Lord Mountjoy to help secure Moyry Pass and the Gap of the North. It is set in the corner of a small bawn and is a rectangular tower three storeys high.

description: National Trust property
summary: Derrymore House is a National Trust property in Bessbrook, County Armagh, Northern Ireland. The grounds are open to the public most of the year round and the drawing room or "Treaty Room" in the house itself on selected dates only. It is described by the National Trust as a "late 18th-century thatched house in gentrified vernacular style".

name: Killeavy Castle
description: country house in Clonlum, County Armagh, Northern Ireland
summary: Killeavy Castle is a Grade A listed 19th-century castle in County Armagh, Northern Ireland. It was built for the Foxall family between 1810 and 1820 and was later designed to resemble Gosford Castle in Markethill, also in County Armagh. Plans for castle's restoration were announced in 2013 with a £1 million grant from Invest Northern Ireland.

name: Clomantagh Tower House
description: tower house in County Kilkenny, Ireland
summary: Clomantagh Castle is a 15th-century tower house located near Freshford, County Kilkenny, in Ireland. Originally constructed in the 1430s, additional buildings and outbuildings were added in the subsequent centuries - including a connected 19th century farmhouse. Carvings on the castle's walls include a Sheela na gig relief.
smr_description: On a low hill with good views from S-WNW and to the E. Another tower house (KK013-033001-), Tubbrid Castle, is visible c. 1.5km to the SSE. According to Carrigan (1905, vol. 2, 368) it was owned by Pierce Ruadh (d. 1539), Earl of Ormond and was inherited by his son Richard Butler, first Lord Mountgarret. summary: Kilbolane Castle is a historical fortification atop Kilbolane Hill, half a kilometre from the village of Milford, County Cork, Ireland. The castle was built in the 15th or 16th century but employed a 13th-century Norman style with high walls joined by circular guard towers and surrounded by a moat, similar to Liscarroll and Ballincollig.
smr_description: At the W end of a low plateau; the ground falls away to the N, W and S. The original form of this keepless 13th-century castle was probably a square ward enclosed by a curtain wall with a circular tower at each corner, but only the SW curtain wall (L 38m), the S and W towers, and a length of the NW wall (L 29.8m) now stand (see plan in McNeill 1997, 140). It is an example of an 'enclosure' castle. The curtain wall (H c. 6m; T 1.8m) and towers were built of random rubble, with a pronounced low base batter. description: ruined castle in County Donegal, Ireland
summary: Inch Castle is a ruined castle located on the southern tip of Inch Island in County Donegal in Ulster, the northern province in Ireland. The castle was constructed around 1430 by the Gaelic Irish lord Neachtain O'Donnell for his father-in-law, Cahir O'Doherty. The Ó Dochartaigh (O'Doherty) clan were the dominant family on the nearby peninsula of Inishowen and had close links with the O'Donnells. It came to form part of the defensive network of O'Doherty fortifications designed to protect them from rival clans and to overawe those who accepted their overlordship.
smr_description: Inch Castle: First mentioned in 1454, this tower house was probably in ruins by 1600. It was granted to Chichester at the time of the Plantation and although his tenant Mr. Skinner had 'pr' pared lyme and other materials to rebuyld the Castle' the remains do not indicate that he made any alterations (Davies and Swan 1939, 205-6; Hunter 1975, 82). Situated on a small ridge on the SW shore of the island, Inch Castle is protected by a cliff on the S and W and a steep slope on the N; the ridge has been quarried to a cliff face on the E, probably both as a defence and for building stone. Only the E half of the keep, three storeys in height survives. The W half is a mass of fallen masonry and the…

smr_description: Situated on a fairly level landscape. name: Ballaghmore Castle
smr_description: In undulating countryside. Ballaghmore Castle may have been built in the late fifteenth century as a residence of the Fitzpatricks of Ossory near a fork in the ancient road known as the Slighe Dala (LA025-018) (Feehan and Cunningham 1978, 117). The castle was taken by Cromwellian forces and partially dismantled in 1647 (Gleeson 1982, 632). Well preserved tower house that was restored in the 19th century and recently revamped. A rectangular-shaped tower house (dims. c. 14.1m SW-NW, 11.85m SE-NE) five storeys high, built of rubble limestone with a slight base-batter. It had a court or bawn (LA015-017003-) immediately surrounding it with circular angle towers. Modern entrance in NE wall…

name: Greencastle
description: castle in Ireland
summary: Northburgh Castle, also known as Green Castle or Greencastle Castle, is a ruined late 13th/early 14th-century castle in Greencastle, a village and fishing port in the north of Inishowen, County Donegal, on the north coast of Ireland. It was completed in 1305 by Richard Óg de Burgh, 2nd Earl of Ulster. Northburgh Castle was sited to control Lough Foyle, and to act as an enabler to de Burgh's plans for expansion. smr_description: Ballybunnion Castle is situated on the summit of a cliff and within the enclosure of a promontory fort (KE004-031001-). It was built by the Fitzmaurices and remained the seat of the heir apparent of that family until the middle of the 16th century. Little is now standing except the E wall, which rises to a height of over 12m. The entrance is on this side, but it is impossible to tell what type of arch it had or how large it was. There would appear to have been a window above it, but both are now running into each other to create a jagged opening in the wall. name: Kilkenny Castle

summary: Kilkenny Castle is a castle in Kilkenny, Ireland, built in 1260 to control a fording-point of the River Nore and the junction of several routeways. It was a symbol of Norman occupation, and in its original 13th-century condition, it would have formed an important element of the town's defences with four large circular corner towers and a massive ditch, part of which can still be seen today on the Parade.

description: castle in County Galway, Ireland
summary: Lough Cutra Castle is a privately owned 19th-century castle located near Gort in south County Galway, Ireland. The castle was designed by English architect John Nash for Colonel Charles Vereker, 2nd Viscount Gort. Construction started in 1811 and was completed in 1817. The castle was later acquired by and a residence of Hugh Gough, 1st Viscount Gough. The castle was purchased by Standish Vereker, 7th Viscount Gort in 1952 and restored by Sir Humphry Wakefield, then husband of Gort's great-niece the Hon. Elizabeth Sidney.

summary: Drishane Castle is a MacCarthy tower house and National Monument located in County Cork, Ireland. In modern times the name is also used to refer to the adjacent house which dates from the 18th century. It is located 2.2 km (1.4 mi) northeast of Millstreet, on the south bank of the Munster Blackwater.
smr_description: Now standing at the SE end of an 18th-century country house, built directly on a rock outcrop. This rectangular 5-storey tower with an adjacent circular 2-storey tower was built by the Mac Carthys in 1450, according to tradition (Lee 1914,64), a date not inconsistent with the present remains. The circular turret was added later, probably in the late 16th/early 17th century to allow for flanking fire by defenders. The adjacent house was built by the Wallis family in the 18th century but enlarged and castellated in the mid-19th century (Bence-Jones, 1988, 108). The house later became a convent school, and is now in use as accommodation for asylum seekers. The tower house and turret were…

The N and W sides of the bawn are obscured by a late Georgian house (Bence-Jones 1978, 74) which altered the plan of the tower house by destroying its W and N walls. name: Shanbally Castle
description: historic site in County Tipperary, Ireland
summary: Shanbally Castle was located near Clogheen, County Tipperary and built for Cornelius O'Callaghan, 1st Viscount Lismore in around 1810. It was the largest house built in Ireland by the noted English architect John Nash. The castle was acquired by the Irish Land Commission in 1954. On 21 March 1960 the castle, after much controversy, was demolished.

smr_description: Situated on flat pasture with extensive views. This gave access to a lobby protected by an overhead murder-hole with access to the spiral stairs in the NE angle and the ground floor directly opposite the main entrance. smr_description: Situated on a small rocky island, c. 300m from the W shore of Lough Sheelin. Constructed in the late 14th century by Thomas McMahon O'Reilly. Davies described it as a two-storey rectangular tower with base batter, a barrel vault over the ground floor and remains of a doorway in S wall. Intramural staircases occur in E wall leading to first floor, and in N wall leading to roof level. Site is densely overgrown with vegetation. The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cavan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1995). summary: Cloughoughter Castle is a ruined circular castle on a small island in Lough Oughter, 4 kilometres (2.5 mi) east of the town of Killeshandra in County Cavan, Ireland.
smr_description: Clogh Oughter castle is a large circular tower situated on a tiny island in Lough Oughter, Co. Cavan. It appears to have been built by the Anglo-Norman de Lacys, lords of Meath, about 1220 as part of their attempt to conquer the territory of Bréifne, roughly equivalent to the modern counties of Leitrim and Cavan. The O’Reillys were the lords of East Breifne (Co. Cavan) and the island on which Clogh Oughter was built had been their royal crannog. In early references to the castle it was called the Castle of Crannog O’Reilly. The de Lacys were driven out of this part of East Bréifne by the O’Reillys in 1233 and Clogh Oughter remained mostly in O’Reilly hands from then until about 1608. During…

name: Castlesampson
smr_description: This is a castle of the Mc Keoghs, descendents of Donnchad Mac Niocal Og (Moore 1974-5; 1987). The castle of Castlesawson had been lost by Melaghlin McKeogh to Irish rebels by 1596 (Cronin 1980, 117) but was sold by his death in 1604 to Thomas Dillon of Curraghboy (Moore 1978, 56). Over 400 acres at Castlesampson was owned by Richard Dillon in 1640, which he retained in the 1660s (Simington 1949, 104). Situated on a rise in an undulating landscape. On the E bank of a NE-SW section of the River Suck, at a point where it turns W. An O'Kelly castle, probably a tower house, was extant here in the late 15th century (O'Donovan 1843, 109-11) at what must have been a fording point (RO041-048006-) as the name suggests. What is described as a bawn (RO041-084002-) at Athliag Maenagan in Hy Many was destroyed by Ulick Mac William Burke in 1487 (AFM vol. 4, 1153). In 1499 the castle, of which nothing remains, was captured by Garrett Mór Fitzgeald, who was the Justiciar and Earl of Kildare, and recaptured by William Burke, who returned it to the sons of William Kelly (ibid., 1251-3). description: historic site in County Laois, Ireland
summary: Dunamase or the Rock of Dunamase is a rocky outcrop in County Laois, Ireland. Rising 46 metres (151 ft) above a plain, it has the ruins of Dunamase Castle, a defensive stronghold dating from the early Hiberno-Norman period with a view across to the Slieve Bloom Mountains. It is near the N80 road between the towns of Portlaoise and Stradbally.

name: Carlow Castle
description: 13th-century castle in County Carlow, Ireland
summary: Carlow Castle is located near the River Barrow in County Carlow, Ireland. It was built between 1207 and 1213, and is a National Monument of Ireland.
smr_description: National Monument No. 10030. Large rectangular three-story limestone keep, of early thirteenth-century date, with circular towers at each angle. Present remains consist of W wall with circular end towers. Built on rising ground with large crennelated stone wall enclosing castle. Main entrance in W wall at first-floor level, now broken out. Similar ground plan to Ferns, Co. Wexford, and Lea, Co. Laois. (Leask 1936, 168-70; AJ 1973, 47-49; Bradley 1989, 8) The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Carlow' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research. Date of…

smr_description: On the flat flood plain of the River Goul at the base of a W-facing slope. The River Goul runs roughly N-S along the W edge of the bawn and then curves, around flowing northeastward N of the bawn. There are good views in all directions, except to E. The tower house occupies the N portion of the bawn (KK008-087001-) which is on a raised platform. According to Carrigan (1905, vol. 2, 299-300), the castle and estate belonged to the Butlers of Ormond, ‘from at least 1560 to 1698, in which latter year they disposed of both, by a fee-farm grant, to a Scotchman named Mr. Hely, ancestor of the present proprietor’. A five storey tower house (max. ext. dims. 13.5m x 10.8m), built of roughly coursed…

name: Rathcoffey Castle
description: castle in County Kildare, Ireland
summary: Rathcoffey Castle is a 15th-century castle in Rathcoffey, County Kildare, Ireland. It is a National Monument.
smr_description: A National Monument. According to Leask, lands in the area were granted to the de Wogan's in 1317 and a castle (KD010-018001-) was probably built shortly afterwards (SMR File). The castle was attacked in 1454, fortified in 1641 (Harbison 1975, 126), and the mansion was built post-c.1785 (Bence-Jones 1978, 239). Prominently sited on the SE shoulder of a hill in arable land, with a panoramic view from N clockwise to WSW and overlooking an enclosure (KD010-016----) c. 500m to NE. A gatehouse (KD010-018002-) stands slightly upslope to NW and low earthworks (KD010-018003-), visible on an aerial photograph (CUCAP BDU036), to the N and E may mark late-18th/19th century garden features. Sections of…

name: Athcarne Castle
description: Elizabethan castle in County Meath, Ireland
summary: Athcarne Castle is a ruined Elizabethan castle outside the town of Duleek in County Meath, Ireland.
smr_description: Situated on a rise in a level landscape with the S-N Hurley River c. 70m to the E. A nineteenth century illustration of Athcarne castle (Anon. 1833) depicts it as a four storey tower house, which has a two storey house attached at the SW side. The house has a return to the NW at the SW end and a large chimney stack rising from the first floor on the NW external wall. Another view (Grose 1791, 2, 33) shows two returns at the opposite (SE) side of the house. The tower house continued to be occupied into the nineteenth century and was considerably altered by the insertion of large windows on the upper floors, but the attached house was replaced by a new wing after 1833 that is still extant as…
